ns2:section.sectionText: Topic: Rethinking Exile: Travel and Displacement in German-speaking Literature since 1945 In the context of German cultural history, the concept of exile literature commonly refers to a narrowly defined body of texts produced by writers who emigrated during the Third Reich. Here, scholars tend to focus on the literary production of antifascist, democratic discourse rather than on the narrative imagination of exile and displacement itself. Taking early postwar texts by returning/visiting ÈmigrÈs as a starting point (Seghers, Arendt), this course examines the aftereffects and new constellations of transnational mobility, including exile, expatriation, immigration, and travel in German-speaking literature since 1945. In order to test the notion of geographical and historical displacement (Entortung) as a productive rather than restrictive space, we will pay particular attention to the relationship between metaphorical, narrative and autobiographical practices; to spatial concepts (home, transit, borders), and to the reconfiguration of public and private memory. We will analyze post-Holocaust, postwar subjectivities through the perspective of geographical displacement (Weiss, Canetti, Sebald); cross-cultural movement related to the writersø investment in and disillusionment with postwar political realities (Johnson, ÷zdamar, Honigmann); and the negotiation of multiple historical pasts in postcommunist travel narratives (Monikova, Wolf, Mora). The readings will focus on literary text, supplemented by a range of essayistic, scholarly, and theoretical texts. Reading knowledge in German recommended.
